extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history, social science, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Methodological guidelines for investigating laws of social progress and history: how to use historical and statistical evidence, distinguish general from special causes, treat causation vs. fatalism, and assess the role of exceptional individuals and governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of intellectual progress
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of human progression in all respects will mainly depend on the order of progression in the intellectual convictions of mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State of knowledge at any time limits industrial and artistic improvements; the speculative faculties and prevailing beliefs determine moral and political conditions. Example: advances in material civilization are preceded by advances in knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for very long historical scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Because progress of knowledge and changes in opinions are very slow and manifest clearly only at long intervals, the general order of sequence cannot be discovered from short periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is necessary to consider the whole of past time—from the first recorded human condition to the present—to identify laws of social progress reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step method: empirical then a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine a law first from history as an empirical law, then convert it into a scientific theorem by deducing it a priori from the principles of human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should combine broad historical induction with theoretical deduction grounded in human nature; treat historical patterns as empirical input to a priori reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comte’s three stages of speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculation on every subject of human inquiry tends to three successive stages: (1) supernatural agencies, (2) metaphysical abstractions, (3) positive science that ascertains laws of succession and similitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this triadic schema to interpret successive intellectual states and connect each to corresponding social phenomena; Mill regards it as having high scientific evidence from history and psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statistical regularities as evidence of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts of statistics show that events which appear capricious in individuals occur with approximate regularity en masse, corroborating the law of causation in human conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: near-constant proportion of murders, suicides, illegitimate births, and forgotten addresses year to year. Large-number regularities provide a posteriori support for causal laws of social phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish general causes from special causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate analysis separates the effect of general causes (state of civilization) from special causes (individual temperament, unique circumstances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The collective experiment (large sample) eliminates special-case variation so the net effect of general causes becomes observable; do not infer from aggregate results that special causes are unimportant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer immutability of moral qualities from statistical averages
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularity in social statistics does not imply that moral qualities are incapable of improvement or of little importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware misreading of statistical invariance: samples often cover narrow geography/time and eliminate local moral variations. Comparing different ages/countries shows wide differences in crime correlated with moral averages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating causation with fatalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Affirming causation of human actions does not imply fatalism or that volitions are ineffective; causation simply means actions are results of human nature and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that human volition is itself a cause and can be a significant instrument; treating actions as caused leaves room for purposeful human and governmental intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human agency and government can meaningfully modify social laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Even though social evolution obeys general causes, human will and governments can convert physical and social laws into instruments of design and have greater power over human facts than over mechanical facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers and exceptional agents can accelerate, arrest, or redirect progress; examples include enlightened Spanish rule in the 18th century producing long-term reforms despite limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional individuals affect celerity and direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Great men and exceptional persons in important positions can decisively determine the speed of social movement and sometimes whether progress occurs at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Newton, Socrates, Luther, Mohammed, Themistocles. Their presence can evoke or instantiate developments that might not arise otherwise. Their effects are often unpredictable and may persist long after their life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on prediction: conditional, not absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical science authorizes conditional predictions: it can trace general causes that render a society receptive to certain changes but cannot precisely predict timing or exactly which exceptional individual will appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science can judge whether general circumstances are compatible with the emergence of transformative figures or trends, but cannot foresee accidental combinations or the advent of great men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility required in generalizations about social evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The order and manner of social progress vary by region and circumstance; there is need for great flexibility when formulating generalizations about the sequence of social states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different peoples under different conditions develop differently; empirical generalizations must allow for wide variation and be confined to appropriate domains (age, country, special positions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Large samples/time needed to eliminate chance
rubrics_metrics.description: To eliminate the effects of particular causes and chance, one must take a sufficiently large field or period so that all combinations of partial causes are included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short periods or narrow geographical samples risk being dominated by temporary or local factors; for stable aggregate measures, expand the field of observation in space and/or time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small or seemingly wasted acts can have long-term unseen effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions that appear to have left no immediate impression may later break traditions or set precedents that prove crucial for future developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: early heretics whose suppressed ideas later enabled Reformers; unnoticed reforms that later seed broad institutional changes. Account for indirect and delayed causal chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great men are not merely early witnesses but active causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Great thinkers and leaders do not only 'catch' truths earlier; they often 'mount the hill-top and evoke' the light—without them some developments might never have occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject metaphors that render great men merely ornamental; consider whether particular achievements required exceptional individual intellect rather than inevitable accumulation.
